newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - France can maintain edge over Germany.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - France can maintain edge over Germany.

text.p: Outperformance of French bonds is set to continue with the 10-year OAT/Bund yield spread capable of stretching further into negative territory by as much as 20 basis points by the end of the year, analysts said on Tuesday.
The French yield curve is still slightly flatter than the German curve at the short end, giving scope for the Bank of France to nudge short-term interest rates lower soon, they said.
At the same time, planned French labour strikes on Thursday were unlikely to worry the market unduly, analysts said.
"There is a bullish backdrop for French bonds," said Steve Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais in Paris.
He said while in the near term the OAT/Bund yield spread might drift back to zero, OATs later in the year were likely to yield 20-25 basis points below Bunds.
At 1253 GMT, the 10-year OAT/Bund spread was at minus four basis points. The 6.5 percent OAT due October 2006 yielded 5.93 percent.
Major said yields were set to rise above six percent for all hard core bonds but because of firm domestic demand, French bond yields would not rise as fast as Bund yields.

Joanne Perez, French strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris, also said French bonds would continue to perform well relative to Germany because of the positive supply situation driving the market. "There are a huge amount of coupons to be paid on October 25, around 44 billion francs, which should be reinvested in the market," she said.

With annual funding ahead of target, government auction sizes would be relatively small for the next couple of months and this would ensure OAT outperformance within the minus five to minus 10 basis point range, Perez said.
But some analysts thought French outperformance had run its course. Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets in London, was sceptical of further spread value for French bonds.

"Over a three-week period we have seen bond yields converge like never before," he said. "If this is a reflection of the political will to see EMU advance on time it is fair enough, but as a result of this the Bundesbank has suddenly adopted a more cautious stance."
He said while the Bundesbank would not want to derail the convergence process, it also wanted to soothe any domestic anxieties that the new euro will be weaker than the mark.
"At the moment bond markets are ignoring this and convergence is still intact. OATs are pushing through Bunds and everything in the garden is rosy," said Roberts.
"But I suspect that more and more those who have enjoyed the ride will be looking to book their profits and in conclusion we will actually get a correction into the year end."
At the short-end of the curve, analysts said there was still scope for French rates to ease.

Domestic investors were keen to tap French bonds and had been removing money from short dated bank deposit accounts which offered low interest rates, to fund a move up the curve to the 10-year sector in search of higher returns.
With this move, Major said the Bank of France would now be less reluctant to allow call money rates to fall.

Analysts said a 24-hour strike in France on Thursday -- called by civil servants, teachers and rail and gas workers against planned government cutbacks -- was unlikely to have a lasting effect on French bonds.

"Because of the positive supply situation, we are not going to see too much selling pressure on the long end," said Perez. "It may mean a pause in the outperformance of the French franc and French franc instruments but that will be temporary."
